Maunder Minimum and Volcanic Forcing: Mechanisms of the 17th Century Climate Dip

Prof. Henrik Lindqvist, Department of Earth Sciences | June 11, 2025

Solar Irradiance and the Maunder Minimum (1645-1715)

The seventeenth century witnessed the sharpest cold anomaly of the Little Ice Age (LIA) epoch in Western Eurasia. High-resolution dendroclimatological reconstructions and Greenland ice-core beryllium-10 isotope records confirm that this cold excursion was driven by a conjunction of depressed solar irradiance—specifically the Maunder Minimum (1645-1715), during which sunspot activity virtually ceased—and prolonged stratospheric volcanic aerosol loading.

Across northwestern and central Europe, summer temperature anomalies plummeted by an estimated 1.2 to 1.8 degrees Celsius below the 1961-1990 baseline average. Growing seasons shortened by three to five weeks, while alpine glaciers, such as the Grindelwald and Mer de Glace glaciers, advanced rapidly down mountain valleys, engulfing hamlets and arable pastures.

Stratospheric Volcanic Aerosol Clusters

Superimposed upon low solar luminosity were major tropical volcanic eruptions, including the explosive eruption of Huaynaputina (Peru) in 1600, Mount Parker (Philippines) in 1641, and an unidentified equatorial eruption in 1693. Sulfate aerosols injected into the stratosphere blocked incoming solar radiation, destabilizing the North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO) into a prolonged negative phase that brought bitterly cold northerly winds and persistent torrential summer precipitation across Europe.
